title: Dealing with racism without hatred
summary: A kind white storekeeper's family versus the places you had to avoid; he saw the hatred as taught sickness and chose to run before fighting.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: But getting back to the kids... It was really very strange. Right down the street, a White fellow had a store named Mister Mack. And his kids were beautiful, you know. And he taught respect for everybody in the neighborhood. No problems, you know. But there were just certain places you'd go, you'd run into it, and there you go -- you got to deal with it. You know, you'd have to deal with it.

Yeah... But you had a pretty good idea. As long as you stayed in a certain range, you were doing pretty good. But if you got out of that territory, then you'd have to deal with it, you know. And I could never really generate any hatred for those kids, because I could kind of understand where they were coming from. They were taught this hatred, you know. They were taught this. And it was a sickness. I could see this. Even when I was a kid, I could see that it was a sickness. So I would deal with it the best way I could. If I had to fight, I'd fight. And run? I'd rather run first! You know?

Yeah, but you had to deal with it, you know. And you'd go down sometimes, you'd be down in town, and one of them would walk over to you and hit you, because he knew you couldn't do anything about it -- because the policeman on the corner was not going to defend you. You know? You'd just have to take it and keep walking, you know. Maybe one day you'd catch him out somewhere! But these are the things that used to go on, you know...
